headlines.article_text: Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile sell off on SpaceX U.S. network plans Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Telecom stocks sank on Friday after Elon Musk's SpaceX announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio. In this article VZ SPCX T TMUS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 5:22 05:22 FCC Chairman Brendan Carr on SpaceX Spectrum deal Squawk on the Street Telecommunications stocks sold off on Friday after Elon Musk 's SpaceX announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio , aiming to expand its Starlink internet into mobile service. Verizon was down roughly 10% on the news, and was pacing for its worst day since 2002. Shares of T-Mobile were down 13% while AT&T fell around 10%, each pacing their own worst days since 2013 and 2000, respectively. SpaceX stock climbed slightly, around 1% for the day. The deal includes acquiring the spectrum from Grain Management, which SpaceX described as a "license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band," in a Thursday statement. FCC Chair Brendan Carr, whose agency will oversee approval of the deal, said that competition in the spectrum market was "really good news for the American consumers" in a CNBC interview. "We're probably going to bring over $100 billion of spectrum into the market over the next two years, so we're seeing a lot of competition," Carr told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Friday. "There's going to be moves in the market. People are going to try to out-compete, out-innovate, and I think that's great. We're going to see how this plays out. It's not for us ultimately to pick winners and losers," he added. Multiple SpaceX analysts lauded the new spectrum deal, with Evercore ISI writing that the rocketmaker "now has the outline of a real network" alongside its existing satellite capabilities. J.P. Morgan wrote that the acquisition made Starlink Mobile's long-term opportunity "more credible." "That said, we continue to see limited near-term risk to U.S. wireless incumbents given the time, infrastructure and capital required to build a competitive terrestrial network," analysts added in a Friday note. Mike Blake | Reuters Elon Musk 's automaker Tesla has changed the brand name of its "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)," or FSD, system in Europe to "Assisted Driving" after German regulators called the branding "somewhat misleading." The package is still sold under the Full Self-Driving (Supervised) branding in the U.S. as a $99 per month subscription for Tesla owners. Tesla is gunning for approvals across Europe, where EV sales have been on the rise this year amid soaring fuel costs caused by the war in Iran, and where Tesla sales have shown signs of recovery from a sales slump last year. On Tuesday, the German Federal Ministry of Transport , known as the BMV, said in a statement that Tesla's brand name "FSD" was "somewhat misleading," adding that "It is not a system that takes over the entire driving task. Rather, it is a driver assistance system that can support certain driving tasks such as accelerating, braking, and steering. The driver must remain attentive at all times." Tesla has been pressuring automotive regulators in Europe, especially in the Netherlands, for rapid approval of their system. Reuters reported that in some cases, Tesla's " browbeating " pushed regulators to reduce the intensity of their safety tests and reviews of the company's technology. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the U.S. automotive safety regulator, is also investigating Tesla's FSD to determine if it is safe for drivers to use in fog, glaring sun or other reduced visibility conditions, and is investigating Tesla to determine whether FSD caused Tesla drivers to commit traffic violations — some that resulted in collisions. In December 2025, a judge in California determined that Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing around its Autopilot and FSD systems, falsely implying they were fully automated driving systems. Tesla has countersued the California DMV to try to shed that "false advertiser" label in a Los Angeles superior court. That litigation is ongoing. In its second-quarter earnings update, Tesla said it had 1.48 million "active" FSD subscriptions but did not say how many were activated from free trials or other incentives.
